CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Chicken — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the drumstick as the food with a built-in handle — matched picture-to-plate and held just like the card shows.

What is this?

A chicken drumstick is the lower part of a chicken’s leg, roasted until the skin turns golden and crinkled. The bone at the end is the handle that made it famous.

What does it mean?

Match the chicken asks the child to connect the card to the real plate — the picture-to-object leap that makes every food card in this room work.

What does the child need to know?

Hold the match honestly: card beside plate, shapes compared out loud — same shape, same color, same handle. The comparison is the lesson; the bite is optional and usually follows.

Why this matters

Drumsticks come with their own grip, so this card teaches holding before eating — the rare food that trains the hand without a utensil.

What it teaches

Picture-to-object matching, grip strength, and gentle animal-to-food storytelling.

Words to learn

chickendrumstickhandleboneroastgolden

Say this to your child

“Same shape, same color — it is the chicken from the card! Hold it by the little bone... can you wave? Hello, drumstick! Listen — hear the crunch when we bite?”

Step by step

  1. Show the card, then bring the plate and lay the drumstick beside it. Compare out loud: shape, color, handle. Let the child hold the real one by the bone and wave hello. Eat a bite and listen for the crunch — skin is the loud part. Finish by asking where drumsticks come from, and follow the child’s lead with the honest short version.

Look closer at the picture

Some children go quiet at the animal story. Keep it simple and kind: chickens are animals, and drumstick is what we call this part of the dinner — no lecture needed either way.

Ask your child

What food is this? Where do we hold it? What part is the handle? Does yours match the card?

What your child can say or do

Drumstick! / Hold the bone. / Same one! / Crunchy skin.

Out in the real world

Drumsticks arrive at picnics, family tables and every holiday plate — the handle-hold travels everywhere dinner is served.

Try it together

Drumstick band: tap two breadsticks or carrot sticks like drumsticks on the table edge — one loud tap, one soft tap — then take a real drumstick bite as the encore.

Understanding check

Show the card and ask where we hold a drumstick. A point to the narrow end, a grab at the real bone, or the word handle passes.

This lesson pairs with the Chicken flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.
